atlas:index/billingPlan:BillingPlan.description: ## # atlas.BillingPlan A billing plan a tenant defines for their app's users (or orgs). The plan's `slug` becomes the `pla` session claim and its `features` the `fea` claim, so entitlement gating works off the plan a subject is on. A plan with no `stripePriceId` is the **free tier** (`free` is then `true`). A subscription's status is written only by the verified Stripe webhook, never by Terraform. Backend API (BAPI): `POST /v1/billing/plans` (create), `GET /v1/billing/plans/:id` (read), `PATCH /v1/billing/plans/:id` (update), `DELETE /v1/billing/plans/:id` (delete). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_billing_plan" "pro" { name = "Pro" slug = "pro" stripe_price_id = "price_123" audience = "org" interval = "month" currency = "usd" features = ["seats", "sso", "audit_log"] limits = { max_seats = 25 max_devices = 5 } pricing_model = "per_seat" trial_days = 14 } # The free tier: a plan with no Stripe price. resource "atlas_billing_plan" "free" { name = "Free" slug = "free" features = ["dashboard"] } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/billingPlan:BillingPlan pro plan_123 ```

atlas:index/cookieConsent:CookieConsent.description: ## # atlas.CookieConsent The cookie-consent banner on your hosted sign-in, sign-up and account pages. Works with any consent-management platform (Cookiebot, CookieMunch, Usercentrics, …): Atlas injects your CMP script and adds its origins to the page's Content Security Policy. A singleton per instance. Each apply replaces the whole setting; destroying the resource turns the banner off. If the banner is turned off outside Terraform, the next plan re-creates it. API: `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /v1/instance/cookie_consent`. ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_cookie_consent" "this" { script_url = "https://consent.cookiebot.com/uc.js" script_id = "Cookiebot" site_id = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" blocking_mode = "auto" extra_origins = ["https://consentcdn.cookiebot.com"] # A "Cookie settings" link in the page footer that reopens the CMP. settings_link = { label = "Cookie settings" preset = "cookiebot" } } ``` With a CMP that listens for its own attributes, use the `custom` preset (or leave `preset` unset) and set `attributes`: ```hcl settings_link = { label = "Privacy choices" attributes = { "data-cc" = "show-settings", "aria-label" = "Open cookie settings" } } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/cookieConsent:CookieConsent this cookie_consent ```

atlas:index/domain:Domain.description: ## # atlas.Domain A custom instance domain (the frontend-api `fapi` host or the `accounts` host). Point a CNAME at the returned `cnameTarget`, then verify out of band. The Backend API has **no update route**, so a change to `role` or `host` replaces the domain. atlas:index/emailProvider:EmailProvider.description: ## # atlas.EmailProvider Your own email provider (bring your own account), so Atlas sends sign-in codes, magic links and notifications through it instead of the shared default sender. Set **exactly one** transport block: `resend`, `ses`, `smtp`, `brevo` or `mailgun`. Secret settings (API keys, passwords) are **sensitive and write-only**: Atlas stores them encrypted and never returns them, so they are kept from your configuration; `secretsSet` reports which ones Atlas holds. Non-secret settings are read back, so drift shows in the plan. Removing an optional non-secret setting from a block keeps the stored value; switch transport (or destroy and re-create) to reset it. Destroying the resource returns the channel to the Atlas default sender. When this provider is the only way the instance can send email and email-dependent features are on (email code or email link sign-in, sign-up email verification, password reset), Atlas refuses to remove it (`409 EMAIL_PROVIDER_IN_USE`) and the destroy fails, naming those features. Turn them off first, or set `forceDestroy` to `true`, apply, and destroy again; the features then stop being offered until a provider is configured again. Development instances keep the shared development sender, so the removal is never refused there. API: `GET /v1/messaging_providers`, `PUT /v1/messaging_providers/email`, `DELETE /v1/messaging_providers/email` (with `?force=true` when `forceDestroy` is set). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_email_provider" "this" { from_address = "Acme " resend = { api_key = var.resend_api_key } } # Alternatively, SMTP (one atlas_email_provider per instance): # resource "atlas_email_provider" "this" { resource "atlas_email_provider" "smtp_example" { from_address = "no-reply@acme.example.com" smtp = { host = "smtp.acme.example.com" port = 587 username = "atlas" password = var.smtp_password } } ``` Each transport is a nested attribute, written `resend = { ... }`. ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/emailProvider:EmailProvider this email ``` Secrets are not recovered on import; the next apply re-sends them from your configuration. `forceDestroy` is imported as `false`.

atlas:index/emailTemplate:EmailTemplate.description: ## # atlas.EmailTemplate The copy override for ONE built-in transactional email template (for example `verificationCode` or `magicLink`). Atlas ships a default subject and body for each system email; this resource overrides the `subject` and/or plain-text `text` for a single template. Atlas validates `{{placeholders}}` at save time, rejecting an override that introduces an unknown variable. Destroying the resource reverts the template to its built-in copy. Backend API (BAPI): `GET /v1/email_templates` (list — the read filters this list by `name`, since there is no get-by-name route), `PUT /v1/email_templates/:name` (save the override — validates `{{placeholders}}`), `DELETE /v1/email_templates/:name` (revert to the built-in copy). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_email_template" "verification" { name = "verification_code" subject = "Your verification code" text = "Your code is {{code}}. Enter it to finish signing in." } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/emailTemplate:EmailTemplate verification verification_code ``` The import id is the template `name`.

atlas:index/entitlementOverride:Entitlem.description: ## # atlas.EntitlementOverride A sales-led entitlement override: pins a plan, features and/or limits onto a user or organization **without** a Stripe subscription — for example an Enterprise contract closed by sales. While it is live (not expired), the override wins over the subscription-derived entitlement, from the subject's next session. atlas:index/instanceConfig:InstanceConfi.description: ## # atlas.InstanceConfig The singleton configuration of the Atlas instance this secret key belongs to: its `allowedOrigins` CORS list and its `authConfig`. There is exactly one per instance, so declare a single `atlas.InstanceConfig` resource. `authConfig` is a **partial patch merged server-side** (never a wholesale replacement). State keeps exactly the patch you wrote (round-tripped verbatim), so a partial config produces a clean plan with no phantom diff; the full server-merged result is exposed separately in the computed `authConfigResolved`. atlas:index/instanceDesign:InstanceDesig.description: ## # atlas.InstanceDesign The design of your hosted sign-in pages for the instance (a singleton): preset, colours (light and dark), typography, shape, card, layout, buttons, inputs, background and logo — the same document the dashboard design editor saves. `design` is a JSON object (write it with `jsonencode`), compared **semantically**: the key order, formatting and `null` members of what Atlas returns never cause drift. atlas:index/notificationCategory:Notific.description: ## # atlas.NotificationCategory A tenant-defined end-user notification category. The `key` identifies the category; the `label` is shown on the end-user's notification-preference toggle. A tenant category is always optional — it cannot shadow a built-in category (`newDevice`, `unattendedAccess`, `credentialChange`) — and is what a `atlas_notification_template.category` points at to gate the template against the user's preferences. Deleting a category still referenced by a template is rejected with `409`; re-categorise or delete the template first. Backend API (BAPI): `POST /v1/notification_categories` (create), `GET /v1/notification_categories` (list — the read filters this list by `key`, since there is no get-by-key route), `PUT /v1/notification_categories/:key` (update the label), `DELETE /v1/notification_categories/:key` (delete — `409` if a template still uses it). atlas:index/oauthProvider:OauthProvider.description: ## # atlas.OauthProvider A configured **social** sign-in provider — a key from the Atlas provider catalog (`google`, `github`, ... ~193 providers). The client secret is write-only: the API never returns it, so its presence is tracked only via `hasSecret` and by whatever `credentials` sets. The redirect/callback URI is **derived** from your instance host and returned read-only — register that exact string at the provider's console. You can also re-brand a provider's button (`displayName`, `iconUrl`), choose its sign-in `mode`, and configure the providers that have no credentials — Steam and the wallet sign-ins `siwe`, `siws` and `siwf` — with `settings` only. > The attribute is named `providerKey` (not `provider`) because `provider` is a > reserved Terraform meta-argument and cannot be used as a resource attribute. Backend API (BAPI, secret-key `sk_`): `PUT /v1/oauth_providers/:provider` (create/update — idempotent), `POST /v1/oauth_providers/:provider/scope` (sign-in/sign-up scope), `POST /v1/oauth_providers/:provider/enabled` (enable toggle), `GET /v1/oauth_providers/:provider` (read), `DELETE /v1/oauth_providers/:provider` (delete). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_oauth_provider" "github" { provider_key = "github" credentials = { client_id = "Iv1.abc123" client_secret = var.github_client_secret # write-only; never read back } scopes = ["read:user", "user:email"] enabled = true allow_sign_in = true allow_sign_up = true } variable "github_client_secret" { type = string sensitive = true } output "github_redirect_uri" { # Register this exact string at the GitHub OAuth app. value = atlas_oauth_provider.github.redirect_uri } ``` A wallet sign-in has no credentials — configure its verifier with `settings`: ```hcl resource "atlas_oauth_provider" "ethereum" { provider_key = "siwe" settings = { domain = "app.example.com" chain_ids = "1,10" rpc_url = "https://mainnet.example-rpc.com" } display_name = "Ethereum wallet" enabled = true } ``` A provider that supports a native idToken flow (e.g. Google One-Tap, Apple) can be configured with just a `clientId` in `credentials` — no secret required. ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/oauthProvider:OauthProvider github github ``` Write-only `credentials` and `settings` are not recovered on import.

atlas:index/orgSettingsSchema:OrgSetting.description: ## # atlas.OrgSettingsSchema The per-instance org-settings JSON Schema registry. An instance registers ONE JSON Schema describing the shape of its organization-level settings; Atlas then validates every per-organization settings write against it, and versions and audits the schema. This resource is a **singleton per instance** — its `id` is always `organizationSettingsSchema`. Each change re-registers the schema and bumps `version`. Atlas exposes no delete for the registry, so destroying this resource only removes it from Terraform state; the registered schema stays in place. Backend API (BAPI): `PUT /v1/organization_settings_schema` (register / update), `GET /v1/organization_settings_schema` (read). There is no delete route. ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_org_settings_schema" "default" { schema = jsonencode({ type = "object" properties = { brand_color = { type = "string" } support_email = { type = "string", format = "email" } seats_limit = { type = "integer", minimum = 1 } } required = ["support_email"] }) } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/orgSettingsSchema:OrgSettingsSchema default organization_settings_schema ```

atlas:index/organizationPolicy:Organizat.description: ## # atlas.OrganizationPolicy The security policy for one organization. Each field is an **optional tightening** on top of the instance policy, merged server-side; a field left unset inherits the instance behaviour (and keeps whatever was last applied), and setting a value enforces it. Atlas exposes no read-only GET for org policy (the org projection omits it), so the provider reads the current policy via an idempotent empty merge. A refresh therefore records an `organization.policy.updated` audit entry even when nothing changed. Backend API (BAPI): `PATCH /v1/organizations/:id/policy` (create / read / update). The read is an empty-body PATCH that merges nothing and returns the resolved policy. ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_organization_policy" "acme" { organization_id = atlas_organization.acme.id require_mfa = true sso_required = true allowed_sign_in_methods = ["password", "oauth_google", "saml"] ip_allowlist = ["203.0.113.0/24"] max_session_age_seconds = 3600 end_user_pool = { enabled = true require_approval = true allow_hosted_signup = true } } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/organizationPolicy:OrganizationPolicy acme org_123 ```

atlas:index/redirectUrl:RedirectUrl.description: ## # atlas.RedirectUrl An allowlisted redirect URL — one of the exact URLs an OAuth / SSO flow may hand control back to. Managing the allowlist as code keeps the set of valid redirect targets under review-and-apply. The Backend API **normalises** the stored value on create (a bare `scheme://host[:port]`, dropping a trailing `/` path) and has **no update route**, so `url` is immutable — changing it forces replacement. Supply an already-normalised absolute http(s) URL to avoid a perpetual diff. Backend API (BAPI): `POST /v1/redirect_urls` (create), `GET /v1/redirect_urls/:id` (read), `DELETE /v1/redirect_urls/:id` (delete). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_redirect_url" "app_callback" { url = "https://app.acme.example.com/callback" } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/redirectUrl:RedirectUrl app_callback rurl_123 ```

atlas:index/smsProvider:SmsProvider.description: ## # atlas.SmsProvider Your own SMS provider (bring your own account), so Atlas sends phone codes through it instead of the shared default sender. Set **exactly one** transport block (a nested attribute, `twilio = { ... }`): `twilio`, `vonage`, `messagebird`, `plivo`, `telnyx`, `sinch`, `infobip`, `clicksend`, `bandwidth` or `awsSns`. Secret settings are **sensitive and write-only**: Atlas stores them encrypted and never returns them, so they are kept from your configuration; `secretsSet` reports which ones Atlas holds. Non-secret settings are read back. Destroying the resource returns the channel to the Atlas default sender. API: `GET /v1/messaging_providers`, `PUT /v1/messaging_providers/sms`, `DELETE /v1/messaging_providers/sms`. ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_sms_provider" "this" { twilio = { account_sid = var.twilio_account_sid auth_token = var.twilio_auth_token from = "+15555550100" } } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/smsProvider:SmsProvider this sms ```

atlas:index/ssoConnection:SsoConnection.description: ## # atlas.SsoConnection An enterprise SSO connection (`oidc`, `saml` or `discourse`). Secrets — the OIDC client secret, the SAML IdP certificate and the Discourse shared secret — are write-only: the API never returns them, so presence is tracked only via the `has_*` booleans and by whatever is set in configuration. Backend API (BAPI): `POST /v1/sso_connections` (create), `GET /v1/sso_connections/:id` (read), `PATCH /v1/sso_connections/:id` (update), `DELETE /v1/sso_connections/:id` (delete). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_sso_connection" "acme_oidc" { type = "oidc" status = "active" oidc_issuer = "https://acme.okta.com" oidc_client_id = "0oa1abcd" oidc_client_secret = var.acme_oidc_secret allowed_domains = ["acme.com"] } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/ssoConnection:SsoConnection acme_oidc ssoc_123 ``` Write-only secrets are not recovered on import.

atlas:index/webhookEndpoint:WebhookEndpo.description: ## # atlas.WebhookEndpoint A webhook endpoint that receives signed Atlas events. The signing secret (`whsec_...`) is stored (sensitive) in state: it is returned on create, and on import it is read back from Atlas. Changing `url`, `enabledEvents` or `active` updates the endpoint **in place** and **preserves the signing secret**, so event deliveries keep verifying. Change `rotateSecretTrigger` to rotate the secret in place. Atlas switches an endpoint off after repeated delivery failures. It then stays in state with `active = false` (and `failingSince` / `disabledAt` set); set `active = true` to switch it back on. Backend API (BAPI): `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints` (create), `GET /v1/webhook_endpoints` (list — the read filters this list by id, since there is no get-by-id route), `PATCH /v1/webhook_endpoints/:id` (in-place update — does not rotate the secret), `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints/:id/rotate_secret` (rotation), `POST /v1/webhook_endpoints/:id/reveal_secret` (import), `DELETE /v1/webhook_endpoints/:id` (delete). ## Example Usage ```hcl resource "atlas_webhook_endpoint" "events" { url = "https://hooks.example.com/atlas" enabled_events = ["user.created", "organization.updated"] # Change this value to rotate the signing secret. rotate_secret_trigger = "2026-10" } ``` ## Import ```sh $ pulumi import atlas:index/webhookEndpoint:WebhookEndpoint events whe_123 ``` The `secret` is read back from Atlas on import (an audited reveal).
